items.context:
Your plant historian produces readings continuously. The team wants a
daily report and a model retrained once a week.

What should the first version of the pipeline be?
items.why:
A report once a day and a model once a week are batch questions, even
though the readings arrive continuously. Streaming buys low latency and
costs you a long-lived service with state, watermarks and delivery
semantics. Nothing here needs the latency, so start with batch and move
to streaming only when a real latency requirement forces it.
items.true: A scheduled batch or micro-batch job
false: A Kafka consumer with exactly-once semantics
Event-time windows closed by a watermark
A stream, since the source never stops

items.context:
You publish every mote's readings to one Kafka topic with several
partitions.

What does Kafka promise about the order you read them back in?
items.why:
Kafka appends each event to one partition, and a consumer reads each
partition forward in the order events were appended. There is no
guarantee across partitions. If you need one mote's readings in order,
they have to land in the same partition. Kafka also knows nothing about
event time: append order is not the order the readings were measured.
false: Order across the whole topic
Order by each event's timestamp
No order at all

items.context:
A consumer reads flow readings from Kafka with default settings and adds
each one to a running total of product shipped.

What will eventually make the total wrong?
items.why:
Kafka is at-least-once by default: a message is never lost, but it can
arrive more than once. A running sum is not idempotent, so every
redelivery inflates it. Exactly-once is opt-in machinery rather than a
setting on the cluster, so assume duplicates and make the processing
tolerate them, for example by de-duplicating on a message id.
items.true: A redelivered message gets counted twice
false: A message is lost and never delivered
Two partitions deliver the same reading at once
The offset resets to zero on every restart

items.context:
Most readings in a sensor feed arrive out of order. You average them in
windows of "everything received between 3:00 and 4:00".

What is wrong with the result?
items.why:
That is a window in processing time: it groups readings by when your
code saw them. When most readings arrive out of order, the 3:00 window
holds readings measured at many different real times, so its average
does not describe any hour of the process. Bucket by event time, the
timestamp the sensor stamped, instead.
items.true: Each window mixes readings measured at different times
false: It reads fine, only a little later than you wanted
The windows overlap, so each reading is counted twice
Nothing, as long as the window is at least an hour

items.context: What is a watermark in a streaming pipeline?
items.why:
A watermark is the system's estimate that it has now seen every event up
to some event time, and when it passes the end of a window the window
closes and emits. It is usually a heuristic, so it can be wrong: a
reading can still turn up after its window closed. That is late data,
and the pipeline needs a policy for it.
items.true: A guess that events up to some time have arrived
false: A guarantee that no later event will ever arrive
The processing time at which a window was emitted
The timestamp of the newest event seen so far

items.context:
An hourly window emits 24.1 degrees. A straggler arrives, and the window,
set to accumulate, emits 24.3 degrees. The dashboard adds every emission
to its daily total.

What goes wrong?
items.why:
An accumulating window re-emits the whole answer, so 24.3 is a
correction that replaces 24.1. A reader that treats it as a new result
counts that hour twice, every time a straggler arrives. Pick the
accumulation mode on purpose and make whoever reads the window agree
on what a second emission means.
items.true: Every late reading is counted twice
false: The straggler is dropped from the day
The 24.1 result is overwritten and lost
Only the hour with the straggler breaks

items.context:
A mote's clock resets every time its battery is swapped. Why check that
its timestamps never run backwards before you compute event-time windows?
items.why:
Event-time windows group readings by the time the sensor stamped. If the
clock is wrong, readings land in the wrong window, and no watermark can
notice. The monotonic check is what earns that trust. Note the last
option: out-of-order arrival is normal on a lossy network, which is
different from a clock that runs backwards.
items.true: The windows trust those timestamps and cannot tell a bad one
false: The check makes the windowing code run faster
Pandera cannot parse a timestamp that goes backwards
Out-of-order readings are always sensor faults

items.context:
A thermocouple reads 24 degrees and passes every check in your schema.

What has the schema shown about that reading?
items.why:
Validation catches the impossible and the malformed. A miscalibrated
sensor that reads plausibly passes, and so does a units error that lands
inside the allowed range. A green validation run means the data is
plausible, which is worth a lot, and it is not evidence that the numbers
are right.
items.true: That it is possible, not that it is true
false: That it is correct to within the range
That the sensor is calibrated
Nothing, because the check is only a range

items.context:
You run `schema.validate(df, lazy=True)` in pandera on a dirty table that
breaks five different checks.

What do you get back?
items.why:
By default pandera raises a `SchemaError` at the first falsified check,
so a dirty table costs one run per problem. With `lazy=True` it
collects every failure and raises a single `SchemaErrors` that
summarizes the offending rows. That is what you want when you are
cleaning data and would rather see every problem at once.
false: A `SchemaError` for the first failure only
The table with the failing rows removed
A warning, and the table unchanged

items.context:
A large sensor feed carries a steady trickle of impossible temperatures.
Halting the pipeline on each one would stop it all day.

What should the gate do with a failing row?
items.why:
Blocking halts everything, which is right only when bad data must never
reach a model or report. Warning lets impossible values through. A
quarantine routes the bad rows aside for inspection and keeps the
pipeline running. Clipping hides the problem: the row now looks
plausible, and nothing records that it was ever wrong.
items.true: Quarantine it, and let the good rows flow on
false: Block, so nothing downstream runs
Clip it to the nearest value in range
Warn, and pass it on with the rest

items.context:
On the Intel Lab feed, one check rejects temperatures outside 0 to 50
degrees and another rejects readings from motes below 2.4 V.

Before you look: how do the readings the two checks reject relate to
each other?
items.why:
96% of the impossible temperatures come from a mote already below
2.4 V. The two checks overlap heavily because they catch one failure
from two sides: a dying battery makes the temperature sensor report
nonsense. A plausibility check on a physical quantity often finds
the cause, not only the symptom.
items.true: Nearly every bad temperature is from a low-battery mote
false: The checks catch unrelated readings
About half of the bad temperatures are low-battery
Low-battery readings are all in range

items.context:
In [`l06-validation.ipynb`](../lectures/l06/l06-validation.ipynb),
compute the thirty-minute tumbling average twice: once bucketed by
event time, once by publish time.

What do some of the publish-time windows show?
items.why:
Bucketing by publish time puts each reading where it arrived, not where
it was measured. Some windows receive nothing, which a dashboard shows
as a gap during normal operation, and the other windows are off by an
amount worth comparing against the tag's own standard deviation. The
event-time windows are the ones that describe the plant.
items.true: Empty windows while the plant ran normally
false: The same averages, only a little later
Fewer readings, but the same mean
Readings from the next window mixed in
